comparison: Both evaluate the core behavioral findings (C3, C31-C36, C66). OpenEval finds the data strongly supported with appropriate statistical analyses. Peer reviewers acknowledge the findings are 'solid' and 'robust' but express significant confusion about interpretation, questioning what the increase in post-reward licking means and noting the behavioral evidence is 'somewhat less complete' than neural data. This represents agreement on data quality but disagreement on clarity of interpretation.

Both address terminal stimulation claims (C4, C66). OpenEval finds these supported by appropriate experimental design. Peer reviewers include these claims in their 'UNCERTAIN' evaluation but do not specifically critique the terminal stimulation data, focusing instead on broader interpretive concerns about the behavioral findings.

Perfect agreement on control experiments (C37-C42). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers find these data well-supported. Peer reviewers explicitly praise these controls as 'important' for ruling out locomotor and inherent reinforcement effects. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Both evaluate pupillometry data (C43-C49). OpenEval finds the data supported with appropriate statistical analyses, though notes the arousal interpretation is somewhat speculative. Peer reviewers express confusion about the interpretation, questioning whether the data indicate independent effects on arousal and conditioned responding. Agreement on data quality but disagreement on interpretive clarity.

Strong agreement on pharmacology findings (C50-C54, C123). OpenEval finds the scopolamine data well-supported with appropriate within-subject design. Peer reviewers acknowledge these findings positively as part of the study's strengths without raising concerns. Both evaluations support these claims.

Strong agreement on GCaMP photometry data (C2, C60-C62, C121). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate controls for movement artifacts. Peer reviewers describe these findings as 'solid' recording data and acknowledge the calcium signals during licking. Both evaluations support these claims.

Perfect agreement on ACh sensor data (C63-C65). OpenEval finds the data supported with appropriate dual-wavelength controls. Peer reviewers acknowledge these findings positively as part of the 'solid' recording data without critique. Both evaluations support these claims.

Strong agreement on concurrent optogenetic stimulation and ACh measurement (C67-C69, C110-C111). OpenEval finds the data supported though notes the gating mechanism is inferred. Peer reviewers explicitly highlight this as 'perhaps the most compelling new idea' showing ACh may have different effects depending on network state. Both evaluations strongly support these claims.

Strong agreement on in vivo electrophysiology findings (C5, C75-C87, C114). OpenEval finds the data well-supported with appropriate statistical analyses and controls. Peer reviewers find these data 'compelling' and 'intriguing,' describing them as 'solid' particularly the recordings. Both evaluations support these claims.

Strong agreement on ex vivo electrophysiology data (C7-C8, C89-C96, C145-C146, C148-C149). OpenEval finds the data strongly supported with appropriate pharmacological controls and cell-type identification. Peer reviewers acknowledge these findings positively as 'solid' recording data providing 'intriguing hints' about state-dependent modulation. Both evaluations support these claims.

Agreement on viral targeting specificity (C23, C163). OpenEval finds the immunohistochemistry data supported with adequate sampling. Peer reviewers acknowledge the experiments were 'well-executed and sufficiently powered' without raising concerns about viral specificity. Both evaluations support these claims.

Both evaluate task design claims (C19-C22, C20-C21, C26). OpenEval finds the task characterization supported and appropriate. Peer reviewers challenge the characterization, with one stating 'I do not think the behaviour in this task can be classed as operant' and requesting additional task details for replication. This represents disagreement on task interpretation and classification.

Both address baseline behavioral characterization including the claim that mice cannot predict rewards (C26). OpenEval finds this inference reasonable from the data. Peer reviewers question the task interpretation more broadly, which relates to claims about predictability. Partial overlap with different emphases.

OpenEval evaluates integrative conclusions about reward-contingency dependence and mechanistic interpretations (C9, C98-C99, C106-C108). Notes these are well-supported by converging evidence but contain speculative elements about 'priming' and 'unmasking' mechanisms. No corresponding specific peer evaluation found, though related concerns appear in R1.

OpenEval evaluates the finding that facilitated neurons had higher baseline firing rates (C88). Finds this supported by appropriate statistical analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found.

OpenEval evaluates interpretive conclusions about cholinergic activity becoming conditioned (C116, C118, C100, C102). Finds these well-supported as interpretations but involving conceptual extrapolation. No specific corresponding peer evaluation, though peer R1 touches on C102 in context of broader interpretive concerns.

OpenEval evaluates integration of current findings with prior literature about licking-related activity (C121-C124). Finds GCaMP and pharmacology data support claims, though functional role inference is somewhat speculative. No corresponding specific peer evaluation found.
